02

RippleA

Three concentric open arcs

The human story — “purpose is multiplied through people,” drawn literally. Three C’s and a ripple radiating outward in one form.

Where it wins

Most meaning per stroke. The only mark that visualises the ripple effect the model is built on. Already built and delivered with the homepage.

What it costs

Busiest of the five. The inner arc closes up below about 24px, so the favicon needs a reduced two-arc cut.

Best used for

Web, print, motion — anywhere it can live above 32px.

03

RippleA

Four variations, shown in lockup
Three arcs, even weightThe delivered proportions in the new palette — navy, slate, copper reading outward.
HairlineThe same form at a much lighter weight. More editorial, and it needs size to survive.
SolidHeavy strokes, no air between them. Reads as one object rather than three arcs.
SegmentedThe arcs broken into fragments. Most movement, least legible as a C.
04 / 07
04

AltitudeB

Three ascending chevrons

The heritage. Air Force, altitude, “Elevating People” — rank insignia read as upward movement.

Where it wins

Instantly legible at any size and unmistakably about ascent. Strong with first-responder and military audiences.

What it costs

Chevrons carry rank and hierarchy. In a clinical or education room that can read as command-and-control rather than partnership.

Best used for

First-responder, defense and public-safety facing material.

AltitudeB

Four variations, shown in lockup
Solid, copper leadingFilled chevrons with the copper at the summit — the most emphatic of the four.
HairlineThe same ascent drawn as line rather than mass. Quieter, and closer to the Ripple in weight.
Navy leadingThe stack reordered so navy tops it. Copper drops to the middle and stops being the leading edge.
NarrowA tighter span, taller stack. Fits a vertical lockup and a square avatar better.

Altitude & EmberEarned authority

Navy carries the depth of thinking; a single burnt-copper accent is the leading edge. Warmer and considerably rarer than gold in this category, and it reads as human without giving up the institutional weight.

The risk

Copper sits close to terracotta and rust. It has to stay a highlight — one element, never a fill — or the palette drifts toward craft-and-artisan.
